About two years ago I went from a single HD6950 to 2 in Crossfire as it seemed to be the cheapest way to get some life back to my ancient Phenom II that's running on a DDR2 motherboard from 2008. Now I think my next steps could be going with some used first or second gen. Ryzen. But seeing how the 3 gen pulls ahead, I don't know... The funny thing is that I probably would only need to buy a mobo, cpu and memory. Even the cooler would fit (afaik) from the AM2+ era. And the old Corsair HX620W should still have a lot of life in it.

Now that I tested the system. It seems that the titles that I could barely play at high settings and 1440p are now running smoothly at 60+fps, so maybe a 1.5 to 2x boost from before on average. Though I haven't tested newer titles. The 3DMark11 (don't have newer ones) score went from P8400 to only around P9700 (for some reason the combined score went down about 300 points) though I didn't even do multiple runs. comments.text:
Get a ryzen 2600 or 3600 with vega 56 or 64.

Someone made a good point: AMD architecture is going to drive the next-generation consoles. Microsoft worked with AMD for the next Xbox. The new PlayStation 5 will use AMD processors.

A YouTube commenter wrote: “I went from a heavily oc'ed (i5) 2500k to a Ryzen 2600 and the difference is pretty unbelievable in both gaming and outside of gaming.”

“My Ryzen 5 3600X surpasses my I7 9700k machine in almost all functions. My I7 machine is relegated to my 7 yearolds Roblox habit and nothing else. Hell, my Ry 3600x beats the I9 in single thread.”

"I upgraded from an i5-3570k (oc @4.2 ghz) to a ryzen 5 1600X and the performance is way better! In games like bf1 or grw it was constantly 100% usage causing me some really annoying fps drops! With this cpu i get a 75% use when the mess is everywhere and normally it stays on 35-45%. Never has those drops again!"

https://www.reddit.com/r/Amd/comments/edzh2k/just_an_quick_update_on_my_3570k_to_3700x_upgrade/
“I would just like to say wow AMD. When I played shadow of the tomb raider with my i5 3670k, I would get probably 15 to 20 fps in the populated cities, making me stop playing the game. I just ran the benchmark on my new pc with the 3700x, and I hit a steady 90 to 100 fps when it got to the market. It just amazes me how much of an upgrade this was when all of the reviews say its just 30-50% better.”

Ryzen only installs on Windows 10. For help https://community.amd.com/community/support-forums/general-discussion

You can use a small screwdriver to put one rice-grain-size blob of thermal paste on the CPU near the center and it will cover the two or three areas where the processor dies are as the paste will spread out when the cooler is placed on it. Thermal paste was designed to fill in the tiny cracks between the heatspreader (CPU casing) and the cooler, not as a primary heat-transfer compound. Too much paste does more harm than good so it's not needed in the corners. Use the small screwdriver to straighten any bent pins too. Renew the paste every 12–18 months. See https://binged.it/2ZL6INa

(If you get the 3600, 2600, 2200g, or 2400G the Wraith Stealth is a bad cooler. Try the Cooler Master 212 evo. Thermal Grizzly Hydronaut is a very good paste.)

The Asrock B450 Gaming k4 has support for Ryzen 3000 out-of-the-box so speak with the retailer first to confirm that they have the new version and not the old. That motherboard copes with the heat from a 16-core 32-thread Ryzen 3950x. In a few years budget buyers will be able to use a 3950x or better from AMD (but NOT from Intel).

A new Ryzen user wrote: “make sure windows 10 allocates enough space for virtual memory because my computer was stuttering for a while”. (I think they mean the page file/swap file. It really means they didn't do so with their old processor.)

“My ONLY point of frustration came from some instability I experienced that took me a while to troubleshoot, first thinking it was probably some sort of memory incompatibility. It ended up being an incompatibility with the Windows 10 Ryzen power plan that was installed. Switched to the regular "Performance" plan and its been rock solid ever since.”

If the processor idles at a high temperature: in the BIOS disable all 3 options for Precision Boost Overdrive (PBO). Set Windows Power Plan (not AMD's one) for "Balanced".

comments.text:
Is "vga card" supposed to mean you need a card with a vga-conector? If yes, its pointless. No modern Card will have that, even HDMI is getting less frequent at the moment. Buy a cheap adapter if thats the case.
1. Ultra setting. Depends highly on the resolution you use. If its 1080p something like a 1660super would be fine (obv. no vga-port lol). For 1440p i would go with the 5700XT and if you really want to game on 4k, then its atleast ! the 2070Super. 
2. Good price. Well of course, all my options have a great price to performance ratio, but this eliminates some of the topend options, cause they get ridiculous expensiv (so no 2080ti).
3. Long term. Hard to achive, its tech, so u WILL have to buy a new one at some day. My advise at the moment tough: buy a card with 6gb or more vram (for 1080p), 8gb would be even better.
4. Good performance: Again, depends what you want to do with them. Raytracing? Well obv. some RTX-card. CUDA-acc. or NVENC for streaming? Also Nvidia. Just the good old regular performance? Look at number 1 above.
5. AMD and Nvidia are choosen.


Overall you still have a lot of cards to choose from:
1080p: 
1660 super (only 6gb vram, but one of the best value options from Nvidia, 1,2,4,5 are all clear, just the long term performance is risky) NOTE: I wouldnt go below this perf. for              future 1080p gaming.
RX 5700 8Gb (Good overall performance, roughly 20-25% more than the 1660 super, but its also more expensiv a bit overkill for 1080p) NOTE: I wouldnt go higher than this perf. for 1080p gaming.
All the other options in between (2060 and 1660ti) have a terrific value, dont get those if they are not on sale. Only if you REALLY want Raytracing consider the 2060.
Bonus for 1080p: The vega 56 is a dying product, but if you are lucky you can get one on sale for about 250$. Its between the other two good 1080p options, but it also is the worst optimized card. DONT get the shitty ref. Card with the blower design and expect to invest some time in undervolting and other things like fancurves. Theoretically its the best value option though.

1440p: RX 5700 or RX 5700XT, no other real options here. Really good value, 2,3,4,5 are safe. Thing with ultra settings though, at this resolution its hard to guarantee them, since they are so demanding. To be safe i would advise the RX 5700XT or even the 2070Super (~11% more performance). 
If you really want Raytracing you could go with the 2060Super (only the super-modell, since the 2060 non-super has 6gb vram!) or the 2070. They have roughly the same performance (2070 is like 5% faster) so get the cheaper one. Still, they offer worse value than the 5700 (XT). 
Bonus for 1440p: There once was a card named Radeon VII with 16gb HBM2. It was released this year and production stopped like 3-5 months after, so its pretty dead already. It is possible that you can grab this card for as low as 500$, not in my region (europe) but in america I saw them once or twice at this pricepoint. Basically its like the vega 56, but more powerfull. You should optimize this card, maybe even undervolt, but its a 700$ MSRP GPU, you wont go wrong paying ~500$ for it. Also its a little noisy.

2160p: Only two real options atm: 2080Super and 2080ti. Both have a non existend value (like WAY too expensive) and the 2080Super isnt even future proof (for 2160p, that is). "Everything on Ultra" is only possible with the 2080ti, but prepare to pay north of 1000$ for it. 
You can "try" 4k gaming with the higher end 1440p options, like the Rx 5700Xt or the 2070Super, but you are far away from the ultra preset at this point and depending on the game your framerate will suffer immensly. 
4k-gaming is realistic if you are willing to take compromises, so medium-high would be your go-to settings, but you should optimize every game you play individually for performance.


I hope this helps you to make a decision. My last advice: be open for more than one option when looking for a gpu, also be patient and search for sales, maybe even of older cards (i gave examples of the noteworthy ones). 
Good Hunting and a merry (early) Christmas.


~Dulindor

comments.text: I'm an AMD guy, have been. Partly because I've gone for the underdog, partly because I would rather buy based on what fits my workload, and performs to the results I need, and not what some numbers on a spreadsheet say. Just as before Ryzen, I was, and have been a die hard AMD FX User. When my boss game me a i7 system, I hated it for running multiple remote logins, calls, conversions, data recovery and backups, Intel just wouldn't hand off between cores. AMD FX processors could multitask far better, and while I'm running data recovery, video conversions, and remote logins, I could still click and run around like nothing was running. Ok, so video conversions took a little longer, but I was able to do more work while running the conversions. So my point in this is how does this card perform to the user as it feels? How does the video quality look?  Run it against the competition and see what it actually feels like and that will answer if it's worth it. Does it melt the paint off the wall watching YouTube? How does it help convert videos? Watch a low resolution video on a large monitor in high resolution and how does the quality look expanding the video? Color quality of the picture? These are more important than how many frames does it get past my monitors ability and my eyes ability. Some of us work more than we play, but still play when we are not working.

comments.text:
TL;DR: Consumer parts lack PCIE lanes and it's stupid.
[Off-topic *RANT*]

Also, am I nuts or just old fasioned thinking most computers should have a lot more PCI-E lanes? I don't think it's unreasonable that a user should expect to be able to put a ethernet card (4 lanes for 10Gbit), sound card (1 lane), and a couple graphics cards (16x2 lanes) without anything slowing down. Even ignoring the 2x graphics cards, which I realize isn't really a thing that the card manufacturers are pushing, that is 21 lanes before NVME drives, which 2-3 4-lane drives seams reasonable to support, so that's another 8-12 lanes. So... 30 lanes seams like a comfortable amount to let people tinker with and upgrade their computers over time. And intel is putting out parts with 22 (up from the 16 skylake launched with) and AMD is using 24 lanes in Zen2. Sure, you can go HEDT with Threadripper for 64, but with latest TR, I doubt they will release "affordable" CPUs with 8 or 16 cores. So if you don't need the crazy multiprocessing, you are paying thousands just to be able to plug a couple extra cards into your motherboard. 

[Queue old man voice]Back in my day...[/End old man voice] you'd put a 2d graphics card, 3d graphics card, sound card, intellegent midi card, ethernet card, and probably a couple others in your board, and nothing would slow down. There were 6-8 expansion slots, and they expected you to use them. I know PCI and PCI-E work differently, and ISA is really different (which sound cards kept using for years after everything else moved on to PCI.) Manufacturers expected you to use the provided slots. Which *makes sense*.
[/Rant over]

comments.text: @TassadarGR  Nvidia's raytrace tech is barely used in a handful of games, and isn't catching on due to the non-standard nature of it. Nvidia decided to pull a Nintendo and produce cards that are, "unique," irrespective of whether they are actually better, and in the process shoehorned two different pipelines into one package that aren't entirely a match for one another. Raster method can render mid-stream whereas raytrace needs to receive the full scene first, objects that should exist as planes or primitives for raytracing are instead tesselated into tiny, fragmented pieces for rasterization, etc. AMD is producing mainstream cards without gimmicks, with a focus on core specs and efficiency only. Why would I even care about a feature that's perhaps supported by one of my games, when I could evaluate the cards based on the framerate and reliability I expect to have across the board? This is to say nothing of the apparent quality compromises associated with enabling Nvidia's raytrace tech, or the vast advantage in Linux drivers on the AMD side, etc. Price-to-performance and low failure rates are reason enough to consider AMD already, gimmicks notwithstanding.

@Zoran EVGA SuperNOVA 750W G1 80 PLUS Gold.  Not sure why I'd need a 1000W PSU just for overclocking a Haswell i5-4690K and a single RTX 2070 Super - max wattage of that card is 269 - the CPU less than half that at full load.  Don't go thinking you need some crazy high PSU just for stable and safe overclocking.  Watch some tutorial vids - recommend GamersNexus FTW.
In 3DMark Time Spy Extreme, I just took 43rd IN THE WORLD in my class (i5-4690K) against all graphics cards on Monday with the ASUS ROG STRIX RTX 2070 Super: https://www.3dmark.com/newsearch#advanced?test=spy%20X&cpuId=1826&gpuId=&gpuCount=1&deviceType=ALL&memoryChannels=0&country=&scoreType=overallScore&hofMode=false&showInvalidResults=false
comments.author: @SemlerPDX

comments.text:
@Zoran 550W is likely plenty, it's the certification and well known brand that allow us to proceed with confidence.  For CPU overclock, you won't ever be adding more than 0.25 to 0.50 additional volts in most cases, and if you're not going for an extreme CPU overclock, it will be your Graphics Card overclock that will be drawing much more power.  On that note, a 550W 80+ Gold certified PSU should have no issues overclocking both the CPU/RAM and the Graphics card to moderate levels.  But don't jump into this without educating yourself first - you want to know your house mains power is stable, so if you're living in a place with frequent blackouts, dips, brownouts, spikes, etc., you will want to invest in a good UPS (uninterruptible power supply) unit that takes power from the wall and delivers it through a battery backup system to your PC.  This product also requires research and education past what I can toss in a comment.  If you live in a good major city with very good stable power infrastructure like I do, you can forgo the expense of a UPS.

When overclocking, first watch general tutorials and read guides on the topic, then find guides specific to the chip or part you want to overclock, as many as you can, and try to pay attention to the common information between them.  A very slight overclock according to the guides should be easy and safe to achieve (even if it doesn't add too much performance) and this is perfect for learning and getting started.  One day, you may buy parts made for this, and then your new skills will really pay off.  Again, I got my $570 graphics card performing at the level of a $1000-1200 card *(minus the extra CUDA cores that come with those models), and I meet or exceed their in-game FPS performance.
